name: Parrot Green
lede: Parrot green names the vivid yellowish green of a parakeet's plumage, and it was also a nineteenth-century paint name for arsenic-copper greens; the names did not always mean the same compound.

sections.title: A bird's green
sections.body: Paterson glosses parrot green as the bright yellow-green of parakeet feathers [1]. The swatch here is far duller than a parrot, a muted olive of the kind that older color charts file under green, and it first appears in our data in Ridgway's 1886 list [2]. Its nearest named neighbors in our graph are [[olive-green]] and [[scheele-s-green]].

sections.title: A paint-maker's name
sections.body:
In the trade, parrot green was a pigment name. Zerr and Rübencamp (1906) describe parrot greens made during the manufacture of emerald green, copper acetate arsenite, by treating the washed emerald green in a cold sugar-of-lead solution [3]. Gentele's 1860 manual instead uses parrot green, together with Mitis green, for a mixture of copper arsenite and copper acetate arsenite [3].

Books disagree on what the name covered. A sample labelled *papegaaigroen*, Dutch for parrot green, in the nineteenth-century Hafkenscheid Collection was analysed by Pey in 1987 and found to be a copper-arsenic compound, tentatively a copper formate arsenite [3][4]. So the same name was applied to at least three compounds, all copper-arsenic greens, none identical [3][4]. Related names with their own pages are [[emerald-green]] and [[mineral-green]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Parrot green appears in 1.74% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 413 paintings, as photographed, more common than 73% of the named colors [5]. Inside a painting it is most often an accent, in 45% of the 235 paintings where we measure roles [5]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 2.2% of the 1,674 paintings from then, 2.0x the baseline of the same museums [5].

The painter most devoted to it is Georges Seurat, with it in 9 of 41 works here, 9.4x his museums' baseline [5]. Aged paint turns green toward this tone, and the earliest match, in 1235, is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not proof of a pigment [5]. The country where it is most over-represented is India, at 2.5x [5].
